sections.h: A worked example of the four states
sections.flag: Illustrative: my own sketch, not a sourced fact.
p: One agent, four moments. Imagine an agent helping with a small product team's inbox and files. Renaming a local draft after a clear instruction is Act: strong evidence, trivial impact, easy undo, so it happens and leaves a line in the activity record. Choosing between two plausible reply drafts is Propose: it recommends one and names the signal that decided it, instead of dropping both on the user.

The last two are different in kind. If the agent cannot tell which of two contacts a message is meant for, that is Ask, and one targeted question is enough. If the next step is sending a message to a customer on inferred consent, that is Stop, whatever the model feels about it. The same agent lands in all four states in one afternoon, which is the point of having a layer instead of a setting.

sections.before: Measure the policy, not the prompt
sections.h: What I would do first on a real product
sections.flag: My opinion, based on the tradeoffs above.
p: List the actions before tuning anything. I would start by writing down every action the agent can take and sorting each one by impact and reversibility, before touching a model or a prompt. That list is the product decision. Most teams I can imagine skip it and go straight to thresholds, which means the thresholds have nothing to be about.

Start strict, then loosen with evidence. I would ship with most actions in Propose or Ask and only move an action class to Act once its record shows it deserves it. Loosening is a visible, reviewable change. Tightening after a bad incident is the expensive way to learn the same lesson, and it tends to happen in public.

sections.h: Where I would not trust this yet
sections.flag: My opinion, based on the tradeoffs above.
p: Reversibility is easy to overrate. An action can be technically undoable and still cause harm in the gap before anyone notices. I would not let the word undo carry too much weight, and I would want recovery cost, not just a yes or no, to feed the decision. Whether a good enough number for that exists is an open question for me.

Four states can become theatre. If Propose turns into a menu nobody reads, we have rebuilt the original loop with better labels. The test I would apply is whether people actually change what they do because of the state shown. If they do not, the layer is decoration and I would say so.
